content:
Implicit schedules feel modern until on-call asks a simple question.

6 min read
Just now

--

Press enter or click to view image in full size

On-call asked a simple question at 3 A.M.
“When does the reconciliation job run?”
Silence in the incident channel. Not because nobody was awake. Because nobody knew.
Six months earlier we deleted the cron entry. The comment in the merge request said: Replaced with event-driven architecture. Scales better. Removes magic schedule.
The event was InvoiceFinalized. The handler was reconcile-ledger. The architecture diagram showed a clean arrow from invoice service to ledger worker. Modern. Elastic. No crontab entry to forget.
What the diagram did not show: reconciliation also ran on PaymentSettled, on a delayed retry queue, on manual admin replay, and once — according to logs — because a deploy replayed a Kafka consumer from the wrong offset.
There was no schedule. There were triggers. Triggers are not the same as a schedule when finance asks why numbers disagree at 9 A.M.
The Cron Was Ugly and Honest
The old world was one line in a crontab:
0 2 * * * /opt/jobs/reconcile-ledger.shUgly. Predictable. Boring in the best way.
Finance knew when numbers would settle. On-call knew when CPU would spike. Support knew not to promise real-time balances before 2:15 A.M. The job was wrong sometimes, but it was wrong on a clock everyone could read.
We replaced it because cron felt embarrassing in architecture reviews. Event-driven felt like progress.
Progress removed the single source of truth about timing.
What Events Hide
Events are good at decoupling producers from consumers. They are bad at answering human questions that start with “when.”
After the migration, timing information scattered:
→ Invoice finalization events arrived continuously through the day → Payment settled events retried with backoff, stretching reconciliation windows → Admin replay buttons existed for support, undocumented in the runbook → Consumer lag meant yesterday’s events processed today → Deploy consumer resets reprocessed historical events without a bright red banner
Each piece was reasonable in isolation. Together they produced ledger states that were “eventually consistent” in the academic sense and “consistently surprising” in the finance sense.
The on-call engineer at 3 A.M. was not failing. The system had no answer to give.
The Incident That Forced a Schedule Ghost
Finance opened a severity-two ticket: morning reports showed yesterday’s totals until almost noon. Not wrong forever. Wrong on a schedule nobody had documented because we believed schedules were obsolete.
Root cause chain:
→ Payment gateway delayed settlement batch on a holiday → Retry queue depth grew overnight → Reconciliation handler processed backlog during business hours → Dashboard refreshed before backlog finished → Executives saw stale totals in the standup deck
Fix was not “add more consumers.” Fix was naming behavior.
We added what I now call a schedule ghost — not a cron replacement, a human-readable map of when effects happen:
→ Earliest reconciliation after invoice: within two minutes under normal load → Latest reconciliation after payment retry exhaustion: up to eighteen hours → Admin replay: immediate, manual, logged → Deploy reprocessing window: forbidden without runbook sign-off
Still event-driven. Now legible.
What We Should Have Kept From Cron
Cron taught habits events do not automatically preserve:
→ A named time when batch effects finish → A single place to look for job definitions → An obvious answer for “is it running” (grep reconcile /etc/cron.d/* vs tracing five services) → Predictable load for capacity planning → A runbook section that fit on one page
Modern architectures can keep those habits without going back to shell scripts on a single box.
Our checklist for event-driven batch work now includes:
→ Document expected completion window, not only trigger name → Expose “last successful reconciliation” metric with alert if older than SLO → Log trigger source on every run: event type, replay, backfill, deploy → Maintain a human schedule summary even when implementation is async → Runbook answers “when” in the first paragraph, not after twelve links
If your runbook starts with “it depends on the event flow,” on-call will depend on coffee.
Observability Without a Schedule Is Guesswork
We had metrics after the cron deletion. Plenty of them.
→ Consumer lag per partition → Handler duration histogram → Error rate on reconcile-ledger → Queue depth on retry topic
None answered “when will finance see correct totals tomorrow morning?”
We added schedule-shaped metrics even though implementation stayed event-driven:
→ reconcile_last_success_timestamp — single gauge, all triggers included → reconcile_expected_completion_slo_seconds — documented constant, alert if exceeded → reconcile_trigger_source label on every run — invoice, payment, replay, deploy_backfill → Morning finance dashboard pinned to last success timestamp, not handler CPU
Observability should answer human questions, not only SRE questions. Humans ask when. SREs ask why CPU spiked. Both matter. Only one gets finance on the phone.
The Audit That Found Five Schedules
External audit asked for “batch job schedule documentation.” We sent the architecture diagram. Auditor sent it back.
Second attempt: engineer spent four hours tracing triggers. Found five effective schedules:
→ Continuous on invoice finalize → Burst on payment retry exhaustion → Manual on support replay button → Accidental on deploy consumer reset → Legacy cron still running on a forgotten VM in staging that prod workers mirrored once during a bad config copy
The staging cron was the punchline. Nobody had deleted it because staging “did not matter” until it did.
Flat recommendation: grep your infra for cron, @Scheduled, schedule:, and rate(. Count how many jobs touch money. That number is your real schedule until documented otherwise.
Flat Truth: Events Scale. Legibility Scales Too.
I am not arguing for cron nostalgia. Cron on one VM does not survive real scale.
I am arguing that replacing a schedule with a graph without replacing temporal clarity is a downgrade wearing upgrade clothes.
Teams feel sophisticated when crontab lines disappear. Finance still asks when. Support still asks when. Auditors definitely ask when.
If engineers cannot answer, the architecture is not finished. It is deferred documentation debt.
Questions to Ask Before Deleting the Cron
Before you merge the PR that removes the schedule, answer aloud:
→ When is the latest a user-visible effect can appear? → What triggers can cause duplicate processing? → How does on-call verify the job ran without opening four dashboards? → What happens to timing on deploy, lag, and replay? → Where does finance look when morning numbers look wrong?
If any answer is “the platform handles that,” you have not replaced cron. You have hidden it.
We still use events. We also have a one-page schedule ghost pinned in the runbook repo. Incidents dropped. Morning finance tickets dropped. On-call answers the 3 A.M. question in one sentence.
That sentence is worth more than the diagram arrow we were proud of in the refactor PR.
The One-Line Answer On-Call Deserves
Our runbook first paragraph now reads:
→ Under normal load, ledger reconciliation completes within two minutes of invoice finalization and within eighteen hours worst-case after payment retry exhaustion; check reconcile_last_success_timestamp before opening a severity-two; admin replay is manual and logged.
One paragraph. No diagram required at 3 A.M.
If you cannot write that paragraph for your event-driven job, you are not done migrating. You have only deleted the crontab line.
Finance Still Thinks in Clocks
Finance software is calendars. Event-driven engineering is graphs. The mismatch persists.
Our controller asked once: “Why can’t this run at 2 A.M. like before?” Flat answer: it can, as a scheduled trigger that emits the same event — a schedule ghost with teeth, not a return to shell scripts on one box.
Some jobs now have an explicit ScheduledReconciliationTick at 2 A.M. that emits ReconcileRequested for anything missed during the day. Event-driven implementation. Clock-visible behavior. Both audiences satisfied without lying to either.
Hybrid is not failure. Hybrid is translation.
On-call now answers the 3 A.M. question in two sentences instead of forty minutes of log archaeology. That alone paid for the documentation sprint.
For background jobs, event-driven patterns, and the operational clarity that keeps async systems debuggable — The Production Engineering Library: The Complete Collection for Production Systems, System Design & Backend Engineering is the shelf I use when someone says “we’ll just emit an event.”
